VIDEO.title: Matthew 12:1-21 – They Studied the Bible... and Still Missed God!
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 12:1-21. On the Sabbath the disciples pick heads of grain, and the Pharisees object. Jesus answers with David and the consecrated bread, the priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath, and Hosea 6:6, and declares that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath. In the synagogue He heals a man's withered hand; the Pharisees plot to destroy Him, and He withdraws, fulfilling Isaiah's Servant song.

Jews took the Sabbath very seriously: in 1 Maccabees 2 some refused to defend themselves on the Sabbath and were killed. The Pharisees were challenging Jesus' halakha, His way of walking out the Torah. Jesus is not abolishing the Law (5:17); He corrects their understanding of the Sabbath's purpose.

Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater (qal vahomer): if the priests can work in the temple on the Sabbath and be innocent, then 'something greater than the temple is here' (12:6). He quotes Hosea 6:6 from the Greek: 'compassion' where the Hebrew has lovingkindness.

Matthew quotes Isaiah 42:1-4 with changes that suggest he is drawing on other parts of Isaiah too, a practice the video calls 'stringing pearls.' The quiet, gentle Servant who will not break a battered reed was not the Messiah many expected.

Why did teachers of God's law get angry when a man was healed? Because they lacked mercy. The Sabbath was God's gift of rest to former slaves (Deuteronomy 5:15); mercy is its spirit, and Jesus lives it out.
The lesson for the original audience, stated negatively: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God.
QUOTES: Lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God.
The spirit that shapes and informs Sabbath is mercy.
God desires a merciful heart in his obedient children.

method.p: The teacher's tip: when someone in the story is upset by something good, stop and ask why. 'Their anger reveals their error.' Then go back to the Old Testament passages Jesus cites and read them in full.

LSB_QUOTES.text: But I say to you that something greater than the temple is here.
For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
A battered reed He will not break off, / And a smoldering wick He will not put out, / Until He leads justice to victory.

src.text: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath, and His disciples became hungry and began to pick the heads of grain and eat. But when the Pharisees saw this, they said to Him, “Look, Your disciples do what is not lawful to do on a Sabbath.”

lines.text: The Pharisees are challenging Jesus' halakha. Halakha comes from the Hebrew for 'to walk': how you walk out the Torah in your life.
Jews took Sabbath-keeping very seriously. In 1 Maccabees 2 some refused to fight back when attacked on the Sabbath, and men, women and children were killed.

Picking grain by hand in a neighbor's field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25); the complaint was about the day. Later rabbis listed reaping and threshing among the labors forbidden on the Sabbath (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2).

src.text: So the priest gave him consecrated bread; for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence which was removed from before Yahweh, in order to put hot bread in its place when it was taken away.

lines.text: Jesus goes to the Tanakh: by the Pharisees' reasoning, David and his men should not have eaten either. So their reading of the Law is off.
Jesus is a rabbi, and rabbis used what was happening around them as springboards for lessons. He is not only defending Himself; He is teaching the Pharisees.
The bread of the Presence was set out fresh every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:8).

left.text: ‘Then on the sabbath day two male lambs one year old without blemish, and two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering, and its drink offering:

right.text: But I say to you that something greater than the temple is here.

lines.text: On the Sabbath the priests changed the bread and offered the doubled burnt offering, and they were innocent. If that is so, how much more Jesus' disciples, because He is greater than the temple.
This is qal vahomer, arguing from the lesser to the greater (the captions write 'kalvahome'). Jesus uses it in 12:5-6 and 12:12, and by it He points to His own identity.

left.text: For I delight in lovingkindness rather than sacrifice, / And in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

right.text: But if you had known what this means, ‘I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the innocent. For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”

lines.text: Jesus quotes Hosea from the Greek Septuagint, which has 'mercy' (eleos) where the Hebrew has lovingkindness (hesed). If you hover over the word in Logos, it shows you.
Jesus has quoted the same verse before, at Matthew's dinner (9:13).

src.text: And He said to them, “What man is there among you who has a sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? How much more valuable then is a man than a sheep! So then, it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Then He *said to the man, “Stretch out your hand!” He stretched it out, and it was restored to normal, like the other.

lines.text: What kind of person gets angry that a law was broken when a man gets a whole new lease on life? Their anger reveals their error.

How could teachers of God's law miss what God was doing in their midst? The answer goes back to the Sermon on the Mount: the heart a disciple cultivates gives insight into God's word and God's activity.

Later rabbinic law agreed that saving life overrides the Sabbath: 'a case of uncertainty concerning a life-threatening situation overrides Shabbat' (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). A withered hand was not life-threatening, which is why the question was a trap.

src.text: You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and Yahweh your God brought you out of there with a mighty hand and with an outstretched arm; therefore Yahweh your God commanded you to observe the sabbath day.

lines.text: God gave a full day of rest to a people beaten and forced into heavy labor. The spirit that shapes the Sabbath is mercy, and Jesus lives it out: mercy to His hungry disciples and to the man with the withered hand.
In John 9 some Pharisees said of Jesus, 'This man is not from God, because He does not keep the Sabbath.' Imagine being upset when God moves in your midst.
Mark adds: 'The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27).

SERVANT.title: My Servant whom I have chosen

src.text: “Behold, My Servant whom I have chosen; / My Beloved in whom My soul is well-pleased; / I will put My Spirit upon Him, / And He shall proclaim justice to the Gentiles. He will not quarrel, nor cry out; / Nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets. A battered reed He will not break off, / And a smoldering wick He will not put out, / Until He leads justice to victory. And in His name the Gentiles will hope.”

lines.text: Matthew gives the quotation to explain why Jesus told people not to make Him known. It comes mostly from Isaiah 42:1-4, with changes that suggest Matthew is drawing on other parts of Isaiah: 'stringing pearls.'
'He will not quarrel' does not mean silence, since He proclaims justice (12:18). It means He will be gentle and humble, not arrogant or callous, not trampling the weak.

SERVANT.title: A crushed reed, a faint wick

left.text: A crushed reed He will not break / And a faintly burning wick He will not extinguish; / He will bring forth justice in truth.

lines.text: This lowly, humble Messiah is not what people expected in the first century, or even wanted, though the Scripture was clear. It may help explain why so many rejected Him.
His goal, for now, is to be gentle and quiet, bringing justice not by violence but through the Spirit of God placed on Him. In His name the nations will hope (12:21).
Matthew 12:18 echoes the Father's words at Jesus' baptism: 'in whom I am well-pleased' (3:17).

BACKGROUND.p: When the Seleucid king tried to stamp out Judaism (about 167 BC), loyal Jews were attacked on the Sabbath and would not fight back (1 Maccabees 2:29-38). Mattathias and his friends then decided they would defend themselves on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:39-41).

The Mishnah later listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden Sabbath work, beginning: 'One who sows, and one who plows, and one who reaps, and one who gathers sheaves into a pile, and one who threshes' (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). It was compiled about AD 200.

Rabbis agreed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath: 'a case of uncertainty concerning a life-threatening situation overrides Shabbat' (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). The debate was over cases that were not urgent, like a withered hand.

The temple ran on the Sabbath: the priests replaced the bread of the Presence (Leviticus 24:8) and offered two extra lambs (Numbers 28:9-10). Work for God's house was never counted as breaking the Sabbath.

DEBATES.p: The video: no, He corrected a wrong reading of it and fulfilled its purpose (5:17). Others say He set aside the Pharisees' rules, not the commandment itself; some read 'Lord of the Sabbath' as authority to reinterpret it.
Matthew follows the Greek Septuagint (eleos). The Hebrew hesed is broader, loyal covenant love; either way the point is a heart that shows mercy rather than rituals alone.
Matthew links Jesus' command to silence (12:16) to Isaiah's gentle Servant. Others add that Jesus avoided stirring up a political messiah movement before His time.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says 'the word consecrated means guiltless.' The Greek anaitios (12:5, 7) means innocent or guiltless; it does not mean consecrated. The point stands: the disciples, like the priests, are innocent.

1 Maccabees 2 tells of Jews killed when they would not fight on the Sabbath (2:29-38), but right after, Mattathias and his friends decided to fight back on the Sabbath (2:39-41). 1 Maccabees is in the Apocrypha, not the LSB.
Jesus' illustration in 12:11 is a sheep that has fallen into a pit, not a lost sheep.

Matthew's quotation is of Isaiah 42:1-4 (the captions first say 'chapter 2:es 1-4'). Many scholars describe it as Matthew's own translation mixing the Hebrew and the Greek; 'stringing pearls' usually names joining passages from different books.
The captions spell Ahimelech 'Aimilec,' Nob 'Knob,' and 1 Maccabees 'first Mcabes.'

QUESTIONS: When has something good that God did ever made you uneasy because it broke your expectations?
What does 'I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice' look like in how you treat people this week?
How does remembering that the Sabbath was a gift to former slaves change how you think about rest?
Where might a lack of mercy be keeping you from seeing what God is doing?
Who around you is a 'battered reed' or a 'smoldering wick'? How can you be gentle with them?
Why do you think the quiet, humble Servant was not the Messiah many wanted?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience, stated negatively: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. The Pharisees failed to recognize their own Messiah, God in their midst, because they were not merciful in their hearts; they were rigid and inflexible, and when God did something outside their understanding they dismissed Him and called His disciples lawbreakers. The inverse is also true: a merciful person comes to truly understand God's word, because God is merciful. Tend to your heart and cultivate mercy by the power of the Holy Spirit, and you will know God and His word more and discern what He is doing around you. It all comes back to mercy and having God's good eye. The lesson is a warning and a call: if you lack mercy, you will condemn what you do not understand and become blind to the activity of God.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, take one Sabbath-like hour to rest and to do one deliberate act of mercy for someone who cannot repay you. Afterward, write down anything you noticed God doing.

## The gentle Servant
1. Matthew 12:15-21: My Servant whom I have chosen
   Isaiah 42 Matthew 12:18-21: "“Behold, My Servant whom I have chosen; / My Beloved in whom My soul is well-pleased; / I will put My Spirit upon Him, / And He shall proclaim justice to the Gentiles. He will not quarrel, nor cry out; / Nor will anyone hear His voice in the streets. A battered reed He will not break off, / And a smoldering wick He will not put out, / Until He leads justice to victory. And in His name the Gentiles will hope.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+12:18-21
   (video) Matthew gives the quotation to explain why Jesus told people not to make Him known. It comes mostly from Isaiah 42:1-4, with changes that suggest Matthew is drawing on other parts of Isaiah: 'stringing pearls.' (Isaiah 42:1-4)
   (video) 'He will not quarrel' does not mean silence, since He proclaims justice (12:18). It means He will be gentle and humble, not arrogant or callous, not trampling the weak.
2. Isaiah 42:3: A crushed reed, a faint wick
   Isaiah (Isaiah 42:3, LSB): "A crushed reed He will not break / And a faintly burning wick He will not extinguish; / He will bring forth justice in truth."
   (video) This lowly, humble Messiah is not what people expected in the first century, or even wanted, though the Scripture was clear. It may help explain why so many rejected Him.
   (video) His goal, for now, is to be gentle and quiet, bringing justice not by violence but through the Spirit of God placed on Him. In His name the nations will hope (12:21).
   [Background] Matthew 12:18 echoes the Father's words at Jesus' baptism: 'in whom I am well-pleased' (3:17). (Matthew 3:17)

## Key people
- Jesus: Lord of the Sabbath, greater than the temple; the gentle Servant of Isaiah 42. [Background] Mark: 'the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath' (Mark 2:28).
- The disciples: Hungry; they pick grain on the Sabbath and are innocent. [Background] Luke adds that they rubbed the heads in their hands (Luke 6:1).
- The Pharisees: Challenge Jesus' halakha and plot to destroy Him; they lacked mercy. [Background] Mark says they plotted with the Herodians (Mark 3:6).
- David: Ate the consecrated bread when he and his men were hungry. [Background] He was fleeing from Saul at the time (1 Samuel 21:10).
- Ahimelech: The priest at Nob who gave David the bread (the captions say 'Aimilec'). [Background] Saul later had him and the priests of Nob killed (1 Samuel 22:16-19).
- The man with the withered hand: Healed on the Sabbath: a whole new lease on life. [Background] Luke notes it was his right hand (Luke 6:6).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Likely the area of the grainfields and 'their synagogue' (12:9); Matthew does not name the town.
- Nob (named in the video): The town of priests where Ahimelech gave David the bread of the Presence (1 Samuel 21:1-6); probably on Mount Scopus, just north-east of Jerusalem, where the priests later offered the Sabbath sacrifices in the temple (Numbers 28:9-10).
- Modein (named in the video): Home of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:1), where the revolt began; the video cites 1 Maccabees 2.

## Key terms
- Sabbath: The seventh day, a day of rest from work (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15).
- Halakha: From the Hebrew 'to walk': how one walks out the Torah in daily life. The captions write 'halaka' and 'hakic.'
- Bread of the Presence: Twelve loaves set before Yahweh in the holy place and replaced every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-9); the LSB also calls it 'consecrated bread.'
- Qal vahomer: 'Light and heavy': a rabbinic argument from the lesser to the greater. The captions write 'kalvahome.'
- Septuagint: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures; Matthew's 'compassion' in Hosea 6:6 follows it.
- Stringing pearls: The video's name for joining several passages into one quotation to make a point.
- Servant: The chosen one of Isaiah's Servant songs (Isaiah 42:1-4; 49; 50; 52-53), whom Matthew identifies with Jesus. [Background]
- Herodians: Supporters of Herod's dynasty, who joined the Pharisees against Jesus (Mark 3:6). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Sabbath under pressure: When the Seleucid king tried to stamp out Judaism (about 167 BC), loyal Jews were attacked on the Sabbath and would not fight back (1 Maccabees 2:29-38). Mattathias and his friends then decided they would defend themselves on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:39-41).
- Forbidden labors: The Mishnah later listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden Sabbath work, beginning: 'One who sows, and one who plows, and one who reaps, and one who gathers sheaves into a pile, and one who threshes' (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2). It was compiled about AD 200.
- Saving life: Rabbis agreed that danger to life overrides the Sabbath: 'a case of uncertainty concerning a life-threatening situation overrides Shabbat' (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). The debate was over cases that were not urgent, like a withered hand.
- Priests at work: The temple ran on the Sabbath: the priests replaced the bread of the Presence (Leviticus 24:8) and offered two extra lambs (Numbers 28:9-10). Work for God's house was never counted as breaking the Sabbath.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Did Jesus break the Sabbath? The video: no, He corrected a wrong reading of it and fulfilled its purpose (5:17). Others say He set aside the Pharisees' rules, not the commandment itself; some read 'Lord of the Sabbath' as authority to reinterpret it.
- Why 'mercy' and not 'lovingkindness'? Matthew follows the Greek Septuagint (eleos). The Hebrew hesed is broader, loyal covenant love; either way the point is a heart that shows mercy rather than rituals alone.
- Why keep it quiet? Matthew links Jesus' command to silence (12:16) to Isaiah's gentle Servant. Others add that Jesus avoided stirring up a political messiah movement before His time.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says 'the word consecrated means guiltless.' The Greek anaitios (12:5, 7) means innocent or guiltless; it does not mean consecrated. The point stands: the disciples, like the priests, are innocent.
- 1 Maccabees 2 tells of Jews killed when they would not fight on the Sabbath (2:29-38), but right after, Mattathias and his friends decided to fight back on the Sabbath (2:39-41). 1 Maccabees is in the Apocrypha, not the LSB.
- Jesus' illustration in 12:11 is a sheep that has fallen into a pit, not a lost sheep.
- Matthew's quotation is of Isaiah 42:1-4 (the captions first say 'chapter 2:es 1-4'). Many scholars describe it as Matthew's own translation mixing the Hebrew and the Greek; 'stringing pearls' usually names joining passages from different books.
- The captions spell Ahimelech 'Aimilec,' Nob 'Knob,' and 1 Maccabees 'first Mcabes.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. When has something good that God did ever made you uneasy because it broke your expectations?
2. What does 'I desire compassion, and not a sacrifice' look like in how you treat people this week?
3. How does remembering that the Sabbath was a gift to former slaves change how you think about rest?
4. Where might a lack of mercy be keeping you from seeing what God is doing?
5. Who around you is a 'battered reed' or a 'smoldering wick'? How can you be gentle with them?
6. Why do you think the quiet, humble Servant was not the Messiah many wanted?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience, stated negatively: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. The Pharisees failed to recognize their own Messiah, God in their midst, because they were not merciful in their hearts; they were rigid and inflexible, and when God did something outside their understanding they dismissed Him and called His disciples lawbreakers. The inverse is also true: a merciful person comes to truly understand God's word, because God is merciful. Tend to your heart and cultivate mercy by the power of the Holy Spirit, and you will know God and His word more and discern what He is doing around you. It all comes back to mercy and having God's good eye. The lesson is a warning and a call: if you lack mercy, you will condemn what you do not understand and become blind to the activity of God.
- Study note (added): this week, take one Sabbath-like hour to rest and to do one deliberate act of mercy for someone who cannot repay you. Afterward, write down anything you noticed God doing.
